title: The City in the Cell: Calabria, the Neapolitan Fortresses, and the Sun that Was Never Built
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Stilo, the birth under the comet
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia; Britannica); birthplace contested and unresolved, a 1968 Italian ministerial decree designates a building at Stignano and the fetched text of en.wikipedia lists Stignano, while it.wikipedia and the scholarly tradition give Stilo; the comet and the caul are tradition reported by biographers, not documents
stops.campa: In a hill town of the Calabrian mountains, far from Naples and farther from Rome, a shoemaker's son is born and baptized Giovanni Domenico at the church of San Biagio al Borgo. Tradition sets a comet in the sky that night and a caul on the child, and reads both afterward as proof of destiny. He learns to give back whatever he has heard once. The friars of the convent school below the town find the boy quicker than his teachers. Stilo is the world he spends his life trying to leave, and the world Spanish soldiers will drag him back into at thirty.
suggested_refs: The church of San Biagio al Borgo, Stilo, where the child was baptized
The 1968 ministerial decree designating a Stignano building as the birthplace, against the scholarship
sources: Luigi Firpo, Bibliografia degli scritti di Tommaso Campanella

stops.name: Placanica, the novitiate
stops.date_confidence: year attested (it.wikipedia); en.wikipedia states he entered the order before the age of fourteen, i.e. before 1582, which the Italian chronology does not support; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: At fifteen he enters the Dominican novitiate at the convent of Placanica, in the same stretch of hill country he was born into. He comes for the books the order keeps and the argument it licenses. The Dominicans give him what nothing else in the province can. He gets a circuit of houses with a library in each, and a formal training in the Aristotelian system he will spend his adult life attacking. Within eleven years the same order delivers him to the cells of the Roman Inquisition, and the charges are read to him by men in his own habit.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Placanica, Calabria

stops.name: San Giorgio Morgeto, the vows and the name
stops.date_confidence: year attested (it.wikipedia); month not recorded and defaulted to mid-year for order within 1583; the age of fifteen conflicts with en.wikipedia's 'before age 14'
stops.campa: He takes his vows at San Giorgio Morgeto and puts down the name he was baptized with. From this day he is fra' Tommaso, named for Aquinas, whose order he has joined and whose authority he will argue against from inside it for forty years. The mendicant education has no single seat: grammar in one house, logic in another, theology in a third, a friar moved wherever his province can find him a lecturer. He is noted early for disputing the lecturers rather than copying them out, and the note follows him from house to house.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of San Giorgio Morgeto, where the vows were taken

stops.name: Nicastro, the schooling in the system he will attack
stops.date_confidence: year attested (it.wikipedia); the full sequence of Calabrian houses is a biographers' reconstruction, the province had no single seminary; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In the Calabrian interior he is drilled at the Dominican house of Nicastro in scholastic logic and Aristotelian natural philosophy. He copies out the syllogisms and does not believe them. Fellow novices testify afterward to his restlessness under rote instruction. The order's Calabrian province keeps no single seminary, so the exact order of the houses he passes through in these years is reconstructed rather than recorded, and Nicastro is named by his earliest biographers as one station among several on a circuit that has no fixed address.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of San Domenico, Nicastro

stops.name: Cosenza, the book that undoes theology
stops.date_confidence: attested (it.wikipedia; SEP: read Telesio's De rerum natura in 1588 at Cosenza); accounts stating Telesio died 'the year before' are wrong, he died at Cosenza on 2 October 1588; month of arrival unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He comes to Cosenza for theology and finds the book that undoes it. Bernardino Telesio's De rerum natura grounds knowledge in the senses and refuses Aristotle the last word. Telesio dies in the city that same year, and the standard account is that the two never meet: the friar reaches Cosenza at or just after the death and views the body rather than a tomb. He seeks out the surviving members of the Accademia Cosentina for their conversation and their manuscripts, and begins the defense of a dead man that will be his first book.
stops.quote: The world is the book where the eternal Wisdom wrote its own concepts
stops.quote_source: Campanella, 'Modo di filosofare,' as quoted on Wikiquote; no translator, edition, or page is given on that page and the wording is unverified against any primary edition [R]
suggested_refs: Bernardino Telesio, De rerum natura iuxta propria principia
The Accademia Cosentina, founded by Telesio

stops.name: Naples, San Domenico Maggiore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Naples years (Ernst 2010; Headley 1997); Bruno's residence in the same convent is attested in giordano_bruno.journey.json, the parallel between the two friars is reconstruction [R]; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He arrives in the Spanish viceregal capital and lodges at San Domenico Maggiore, the great Dominican house at the center of the city's religious life. Giordano Bruno wore this habit in this same convent and fled it under a heresy charge fourteen years earlier. Campanella is drawn into the circle around Giovanni Battista della Porta, natural magician and playwright, where astrology and magic are argued against the reigning curriculum. Naples is thick with censors and informers, and his outspokenness in that circle is noted from the first month.
suggested_refs: The convent of San Domenico Maggiore, Naples, house of both Bruno and Campanella
Giovanni Battista della Porta, Magia naturalis
sources: John Headley, Tommaso Campanella and the Transformation of the World (1997)

stops.name: Naples, the first cell
stops.date_confidence: book completed August 1589, arrest dated 1591 (it.wikipedia; en.wikipedia); the month of the arrest is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: Philosophia sensibus demonstrata is published, a defense of Telesio's empiricism against an Aristotelian critic, and its author is denounced to the Neapolitan Inquisition. The charge as recorded runs to demonic practice as well as suspect philosophy. He is imprisoned in Naples, briefly, and released marked: the surveillance file opened on him in these months follows him into every later city he enters. It is his first cell. He will spend the greater part of the next thirty-five years in one or another of them.
suggested_refs: Campanella, Philosophia sensibus demonstrata (1591)

segments.name: North, One Stage Ahead of the Agents

stops.name: Naples, the tribunal and the order to Altomonte
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia); the earlier Altomonte student posting rests on order registers cited by Amabile (1882) and not independently verified [R], and an account naming the house there as 'San Francesco' is wrong, that foundation is Minim
stops.campa: A Dominican tribunal sentences him and orders him back to the convent at Altomonte in northern Calabria, a house on the circuit of his own student years. He does not go. Refusing an order of his own order turns a friar under suspicion into a fugitive. The next six years he spends on the road and in other men's cities. Within days he is on the road north with letters of introduction in his baggage and the papers of an unfinished book, in a country where every diocese can write to every other.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Altomonte, the house he was ordered to and refused

stops.name: Florence, the audience with Ferdinando I
stops.date_confidence: the journey is attested (it.wikipedia); the substance of the audience is disputed between accounts, some inflating it into a courtship of Medici patronage and others treating it as a courtesy stop, and is not adjudicated; day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He travels north and is received at the Medici court, where he has an audience with Grand Duke Ferdinando I. Accounts differ on what passes between them. Some inflate the meeting into a serious courtship of Medici patronage; others treat it as a courtesy stop on a road he is already taking at speed. He does not stay. A friar under an unexecuted sentence cannot linger anywhere a nuncio might write to, and within weeks he is moving again, toward Bologna and the university cities of the north.
suggested_refs: The court of Grand Duke Ferdinando I de' Medici, Florence

stops.name: Bologna, the manuscripts seized
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1592 (it.wikipedia; Ernst 2010); day unknown, defaulted; the contents of the lost manuscripts are a gap no source fills
stops.campa: On the road to Padua an agent of the Inquisition takes his travelling papers, unpublished manuscripts among them. Some of the seized writings never resurface and are presumed lost; what they contained is a gap no source fills. For the next two years he moves from city to city, one stage ahead of the officials who open his notebooks before he does. He reaches Padua with his argument intact and his evidence confiscated, and begins the work again from memory.
suggested_refs: The Inquisition's Bologna seizure of Campanella's travelling papers, October 1592

stops.name: Padua, the meeting with Galileo
stops.date_confidence: attested (it.wikipedia; SEP); accounts claiming the two never met, and that the acquaintance is only inferred from later correspondence, are contradicted by both sources; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Padua is a university city under Venetian jurisdiction, further from Rome's reach than anywhere he has lived. He meets the philosopher Andrea Chiocco and, at the same university, the young professor of mathematics Galileo Galilei, who holds the chair Giordano Bruno had wanted and been refused. Twenty-three years later Campanella will write this man's defense from a Neapolitan cell, and eleven years after that Galileo will abjure in the Roman church where Campanella abjured first. Venetian jurisdiction keeps Rome off him for a year, and no longer.
suggested_refs: The University of Padua under Venetian jurisdiction
Andrea Chiocco, physician and philosopher of Verona

stops.name: Padua, the two proceedings
stops.date_confidence: SEP gives 'arrested at the beginning of 1594' and it.wikipedia separates the two cases; secondary accounts routinely fold them into a single 1593 denunciation on two charges, which is refused here; exact day not recorded, defaulted
stops.campa: Early in 1593 he is investigated at the convent of Sant'Agostino over a sodomy incident and is cleared. The arrest that matters is a separate matter and later: co-authorship of the De tribus impostoribus, Democritean atheism, opposition to ecclesiastical authority. He is tortured at Padua alongside Ottavio Longo and Giovan Battista Clario. The two proceedings are commonly folded together into one denunciation on two charges. They were not one. The first was closed before the second was opened.
suggested_refs: The clandestine De tribus impostoribus, whose co-authorship was charged against him
The convent of Sant'Agostino, Padua

stops.name: Rome, delivered to the Holy Office
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia); the coordinates are for the Holy Office prison beside the Vatican and are derived here, no Rome pin was inherited from an existing atlas file
stops.campa: On the eleventh of October he is handed to the Roman Inquisition and lodged in the prison of the Holy Office beside the Vatican. Venetian and Roman jurisdictions have disputed the right to try him, and Rome has won the argument. The examinations reach back through Naples and Padua: natural philosophy, astrology, the mortality of the soul, the natural origin of religion. He is twenty-six years old and has now been in custody in three cities, and the file that opened in Naples in 1591 is on the table in front of him.
suggested_refs: The prison of the Holy Office, Rome, in the Palazzo del Sant'Uffizio

stops.name: Rome, the torture of April 1595
stops.date_confidence: month attested (it.wikipedia), day not recorded and defaulted; the count of seven tortures across all trials is en.wikipedia's and is not itemized there [R]
stops.campa: He is put to torture in the course of the Roman proceedings. What he says under it the trial records hold, and the sources reachable here do not quote them. He does not break in the way his examiners require. The tribunal, unable to convict him of formal heresy, turns to the lesser instrument: an abjuration that concedes grave suspicion without conceding the crime. Of the seven times he is tortured across his several trials, this is the second, and there are five more waiting in a city he has not seen yet.
suggested_refs: The Roman Inquisition's procedural distinction between abjuration de vehementi and de formali

stops.name: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, the abjuration de vehementi
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia); accounts dating this abjuration to 1597 conflate two separate Roman trials, the first closed in 1595 and the second in December 1597
stops.campa: In the Dominican church at the heart of Rome he abjures de vehementi, the renunciation made by a man vehemently suspected of heresy, one degree short of the harshest finding the tribunal can hand down. He kneels in his own order's principal Roman church to do it. Thirty-four years later, absolved at last, he will live in the convent attached to this same building as a free man. Thirty-eight years later Galileo will kneel in this nave and abjure in his turn, and Campanella will still be defending him.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome, site of both Campanella's 1595 abjuration and Galileo's in 1633

stops.name: Santa Sabina, the confinement on the Aventine
stops.date_confidence: confinement and the release of 31 December 1596 attested (it.wikipedia); the day of entry is inferred as the day after the abjuration and is reconstruction [R]
stops.campa: He is confined to the Dominican convent on the Aventine, above the river, and held there through 1596. The regime is a convent's rather than a prison's, but he is not free to leave and not free to write what he likes. He is released on the last day of December 1596, after nineteen months. Nine weeks of liberty follow. Then the whole Roman sequence begins again from the top: denunciation, arrest, examination, and a second tribunal that knows exactly what the first one found.
suggested_refs: The convent of Santa Sabina on the Aventine, Dominican house of confinement

stops.name: Rome, the denunciation of Prestinace
stops.date_confidence: arrest of 5 March and acquittal of 17 December 1597 both attested (it.wikipedia; SEP)
stops.campa: A condemned criminal named Scipione Prestinace denounces him, and he is arrested for the third time in six years. The case collapses. On the seventeenth of December he is acquitted, ordered to write nothing further, and released into the custody of his superiors, who are to keep him in Calabria under supervision. He is twenty-nine, has been tried three times and tortured twice, and has been forbidden by a Roman tribunal to put anything on paper for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The 17 December 1597 sentence of acquittal with the prohibition on writing

stops.name: Naples, the road south
stops.date_confidence: month attested (it.wikipedia); day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He passes through Naples in July and takes the road into Calabria, back to the province he left as a fugitive six years earlier. His superiors are charged with keeping him quiet in a convent. Within thirteen months he will be organizing an armed rising against the Spanish crown, preaching the end of the old order from a pulpit in his birthplace, and reading the conjunctions for the year 1600. The prohibition on writing holds for exactly as long as it takes him to reach the mountains.
suggested_refs: The Spanish viceregal administration of Calabria under Philip II

stops.name: Stilo, Santa Maria di Gesu
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia; SEP)
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption he arrives in his own birthplace and takes residence at the convent of Santa Maria di Gesu, a supervised friar in the town where a comet is supposed to have marked his birth. The province he returns to is chafing under Spanish taxation and viceregal misrule. He resumes preaching. The supervision, whatever form it takes on paper, does not extend to what a famous man says from a pulpit to listeners who have their own reasons for hearing him out.
suggested_refs: The convent of Santa Maria di Gesu, Stilo

stops.name: Catanzaro, the network in the provincial capital
stops.date_confidence: the organizing is attested (Amabile 1882; it.wikipedia; en.wikipedia) but is known largely through the prosecution's own record; the extent of any Ottoman negotiation is therefore [R]; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He rides the Calabrian towns building a network of clergy, minor nobles, and disaffected subjects, and Catanzaro, the provincial capital, is one of his organizing stops. He preaches an apocalyptic astrology: the conjunctions read that 1600 brings down the old order entire. Trial testimony has him negotiating for Ottoman naval support to back the rising. What he means to raise in the ruins he has already begun to describe, a city governed by knowledge, its goods held in common, its magistrates chosen for what they know.
stops.quote: war is decided on. Immediately after a priest, whom they call Forensic, is sent away.
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 245
suggested_refs: The trial record of the 1599 Calabrian conspiracy, the fullest source for its organization

stops.name: Squillace, the clerical recruits
stops.date_confidence: that Squillace clergy joined is attested (Amabile 1882) but the depth of organization is disputed among historians [R]; accounts naming Dionisio Ponzio and a 'Giovanni Battista Pisano' as the informers are wrong, Treccani's Firpo gives Fabio di Lauro and Giambattista Biblia; month approximate, defaulted
stops.campa: The diocese of Squillace furnishes several of the conspiracy's clerical recruits, drawn by the mixture of millenarian astrology and grievance against Spanish taxation. How deep the organization goes there, as against a scatter of individual sympathizers, is disputed among historians and documented mainly through the prosecution's own record. Dionisio Ponzio, one of the leading conspirators, escapes and is never taken. The men who inform are others, and they inform in August, and their names are in the register.
stops.quote: no one in the fraternity can do injury to another.
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 231
suggested_refs: The diocese of Squillace and its clergy in the 1599 conspiracy trial
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, entry by Luigi Firpo (1974)

stops.name: Stilo, the rising betrayed
stops.date_confidence: denunciation dates attested (Treccani/Firpo: di Lauro and Biblia on 10 August, fra' Cornelio da Nizza on 14 August); the intended date of the rising itself is known only from the prosecution's reconstruction [R]
stops.campa: The revolt is timed by his own calculations to a favorable configuration in late summer. On the tenth of August Fabio di Lauro and Giambattista Biblia denounce the conspiracy; fra' Cornelio da Nizza follows on the fourteenth. Spanish reinforcements move first and the rising never breaks. Not one battle is fought. Dozens of participants are tried in the months after and several are executed, and the philosopher who read the sky for the year of the world's renewal has read it, in the only sense his judges care about, wrong.
stops.quote: If You return to earth, come armed—Lord—because enemies are preparing other crosses—not Turks, not Jews—but those of Your own kingdom
stops.quote_source: Campanella, 'To Jesus Christ,' in Sherry Roush, Selected Philosophical Poems of Tommaso Campanella (University of Chicago Press, 2011), p. 18, as printed on en.wikiquote; Roush p. 18 could not be inspected directly (Google Books rate-limited 429, HathiTrust and Internet Archive search-inside both 403), so the page citation is Wikiquote's word and the dashes are as that page prints them
suggested_refs: The denunciations of 10 and 14 August 1599 in the Calabrian trial record

stops.name: Stignano and Titi, the three weeks in hiding
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia); coordinates are for Stignano, the second hiding place at Titi is not separately pinned
stops.campa: With Spanish troops arriving he leaves the convent and hides in the countryside around Stignano and Titi, in the hill villages of his own childhood, sheltered by men who have not yet been questioned. He is a fugitive friar in the one province where every stone is known to him and every road is watched by people who know him too. The hiding lasts three weeks. Stignano is the same village a ministerial decree will name, three hundred and sixty-nine years later, as the place he was born.
suggested_refs: The villages of Stignano and Titi in the Stilo hinterland

stops.name: Castelvetere, the capture
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia; Treccani names Antonio Mesuraca as the man who gave him up on 6 September); Castelvetere is the modern Caulonia
stops.campa: Antonio Mesuraca gives him up on the sixth of September, and Spanish forces take him and carry him down to Castelvetere on the coast. The Calabrian phase of the case ends here. What begins is a transfer through custody, from provincial soldiers to the viceregal apparatus at Naples, that will take two months. He is thirty-one. He will not stand outside a prison wall again until he is fifty-seven, and the first country he sees as a free old man will not be Italy.
suggested_refs: Castelvetere, now Caulonia, first place of custody after the capture

stops.name: Naples, Castel Nuovo, the identification
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia gives the formal identification at Castel Nuovo on 23 November 1599, Treccani puts his arrival in Naples on 8 November; accounts placing him in Castel Nuovo in September confuse this with the Calabrian capture
stops.campa: He reaches Naples custody in November and is formally identified at Castel Nuovo, the Angevin fortress that serves as the city's chief state prison. The charges are lese-majesty and heresy folded into one capital case; either alone would be enough to kill him. He does the arithmetic at once. A heresy conviction means the fire, and a finding of insanity means life. He sets about constructing a madman for his judges to examine, and the trial record he leaves behind shows how deliberately it is done.
suggested_refs: Castel Nuovo, Naples, first and last of his Neapolitan prisons

stops.name: Castel Nuovo, fourteen months of madness
stops.date_confidence: the feigned madness begins 2 April 1600 and runs fourteen months, in Castel Nuovo (Treccani/Firpo); La Monarchia di Spagna is dated 1600 (it.wikipedia, en.wikipedia), with an earlier lost redaction from the Padua years, and accounts dating it 1607-1608 are wrong
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of February the Holy Office burns Giordano Bruno at Campo de' Fiori in Rome. On the second of April, in a Naples cell, Campanella begins to perform insanity and sustains the performance fourteen months: incoherent answers to interrogators, a straw mattress set alight, a body that will not respond the way a sane body responds. In the same year he writes La Monarchia di Spagna, arguing for a Spanish-led universal monarchy under papal guidance, from a prison of the crown he had raised Calabria against.
suggested_refs: Campanella, La Monarchia di Spagna (1600)
The burning of Giordano Bruno at Campo de' Fiori, 17 February 1600

stops.name: Castel Nuovo, the veglia
stops.date_confidence: date and place attested (Treccani/Firpo, from the trial records: Castel Nuovo, 4-5 June 1601); duration contradicted and not resolved, Firpo gives thirty-six consecutive hours and it.wikipedia gives roughly forty; accounts setting the veglia at Castel Sant'Elmo are wrong, he was not held there until July 1604
stops.campa: To prove the madness a sham the tribunal puts him to the veglia, a torture of suspension and enforced sleeplessness, the severest instrument the Neapolitan court uses short of killing a man. He does not break. The judges accept in the end that whoever holds out under it is not feigning, and the capital sentence does not fall. He is broken and infirm for six months afterward and carries the injury into his later writings and petitions. It is the fourth time he has been tortured, and the last.
stops.quote: No one is killed or stoned unless by the hands of the people
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 258, on capital punishment among the Solarians
suggested_refs: The veglia of 4-5 June 1601 as recorded in the Neapolitan trial records

stops.name: Castel Nuovo, La citta del sole
stops.date_confidence: year and place attested (Treccani: he passes 1602 composing the Citta del Sole, in Castel Nuovo, three years before the Sant'Elmo transfer); accounts setting the composition at Castel Sant'Elmo are wrong; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He spends the year composing, in a cell, under sentence, the description of a city that does not exist: ruled by a priest called Hoh whom we should call Metaphysic, governed under him by three co-rulers named Power, Wisdom, and Love, its goods held in common, its marriages assigned by astrologers, its walls painted with the whole of the sciences so that children learn them by walking. He writes it in Italian first. Plato's republic is the ancestor the book never troubles to hide.
stops.quote: no one can appropriate anything to himself
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 230
suggested_refs: Campanella, La citta del sole, Italian text of 1602
Plato, Republic, the ancestor of the Solarian constitution

stops.name: Castel Sant'Elmo, the blind cell
stops.date_confidence: transfer attested to July 1604 (Treccani), held four years in an underground cell in irons; Atheismus triumphatus composed 1605-1607 per it.wikipedia and 1606-1607 per SEP, the single year 1605 given in some accounts is too narrow; day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In July he is moved up the hill to Castel Sant'Elmo and put into a blind underground pit, damp, in irons at hands and feet, and held there four years. Here he composes the Atheismus triumphatus, refuting atheism on naturalistic and providential grounds, and works at the Metaphysica that will occupy him for decades. The conditions are the worst of the twenty-seven years, and the writing does not stop for them. He has no library. He writes out of what his memory holds.
stops.quote: I learn more from the anatomy of an ant or a blade of grass...than from all the books which have been written since the beginning of time.
stops.quote_source: Campanella, letter of 1607, as cited in Elizabeth L. Eisenstein, The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe (Cambridge University Press, 2012), p. 218, via Wikiquote; the 1607 letter itself was not located or fetched, so this is a secondary citation only [R]
suggested_refs: Campanella, Atheismus triumphatus (composed 1605-1607)
Castel Sant'Elmo, Naples, and its underground cells

stops.name: Castel dell'Ovo, the lighter years and Adami's visit
stops.date_confidence: Castel dell'Ovo dated 1608-1614 by Treccani, under lighter conditions with visitors and writing allowed; Adami's visit dated 1612 by SEP; accounts placing Castel dell'Ovo in 1604 have swapped this transfer with the Sant'Elmo transfer of July 1604; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: From 1608 he is held in the seafront fortress under a lighter regime: visitors, books, room to write. The German scholar Tobias Adami comes to the cell in 1612, takes copies away with him, and prints Campanella in Germany, so that a prisoner of the Spanish crown acquires a European readership while the crown still has him in irons. He works at the Theologia. The order of transfers among the Naples prisons is reconstructed from petitions and letters; no continuous prison register survives.
suggested_refs: Tobias Adami's German editions of Campanella, printed from prison copies
Castel dell'Ovo, Naples

stops.name: Castel Sant'Elmo, the Apologia pro Galileo
stops.date_confidence: Treccani places the composition at Castel Sant'Elmo in 1616, which sits awkwardly against the same source's Sant'Elmo dating of 1604-1608; the strain is flagged and not resolved; published 1622; claims that Campanella and Galileo never met contradict the attested Padua meeting of 1593; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The year Rome admonishes Galileo, Campanella writes the defense from prison: that heliocentrism contradicts no scripture properly interpreted, and that nature must be free to be investigated by observation. He met the man once, at Padua, twenty-three years earlier, and has been in cells ever since. He has every reason to keep his head down and does not. The book is published in 1622 in Germany. In 1633 Galileo abjures in the Roman church where Campanella abjured in 1595, and Campanella keeps defending him.
suggested_refs: Campanella, Apologia pro Galileo (written 1616, published Frankfurt 1622)

stops.name: Castel Nuovo, the release
stops.date_confidence: date and place attested (Treccani: released 23 May 1626 from Castel Nuovo after almost twenty-seven years; SEP concurs on the prison); accounts naming Castel Sant'Elmo as the prison of release are wrong; sources differ on whether to count the twenty-seven years from the 1599 arrest or the sentencing after the 1601 torture
stops.campa: After almost twenty-seven years he walks out of Castel Nuovo, released through the intercession of Cardinal Maffeo Barberini, who is now Urban VIII. He is fifty-seven. He went into these fortresses a Calabrian conspirator; he comes out the author of a utopia, a defense of Galileo, a metaphysics, and a theology, most of it written in irons and smuggled out by visitors. The release is not liberty. Rome reclaims jurisdiction at once, and he goes north in custody to have the old heresy questions settled.
suggested_refs: The intercession of Cardinal Maffeo Barberini, later Urban VIII, in Campanella's release

segments.name: Rome, the Astrologer of Urban VIII

stops.name: Rome, Castel Sant'Angelo and the second detention
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the standard itinerary (Amabile 1882; Bonansea 1969), the exact duration of the Sant'Angelo stop is not independently confirmed [R]; the lighter Roman supervision of 1627-1629 is attested (Bonansea; Ernst 2010); day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: On arrival in Rome he is held in the papal fortress on the Tiber, the stage between Neapolitan and Roman custody. The stop is short, days rather than years, and then the case passes formally to the Holy Office for a fresh examination that runs nearly three years. The conditions are nothing like Naples: visitors, books, in time lodging outside strict confinement. The tribunal that once tortured him has begun to be more interested in his astrology than in his heresies, and the case moves toward absolution.
stops.quote: He must also be well read in the Prophets and in astrology.
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 234, on the required learning of the ruler Hoh
suggested_refs: Castel Sant'Angelo, Rome, papal fortress and state prison

stops.name: The Vatican Apostolic Palace, the eclipse rite
stops.date_confidence: attested from Campanella's own account in De siderali fato vitando, cited in Ernst (2010) and Headley (1997); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Urban VIII fears that a coming solar eclipse portends his death and sends for the friar his own tribunal spent thirty years prosecuting. In the sealed papal apartment they burn laurel and rosemary, light two candles and five torches for the seven planets, and order the room to draw the beneficial influence and turn aside the harm the sky is sending. Campanella writes the procedure down himself. The astrology that convicted him in Calabria is now performed at the top of the Church, by its author, for the pope.
stops.quote: a room sealed against outside air, laurel and rosemary burned, two candles and five torches lit for the seven planets
stops.quote_source: Campanella, De siderali fato vitando, as cited in Germana Ernst, Tommaso Campanella (2010) and John Headley, Tommaso Campanella and the Transformation of the World (1997)
suggested_refs: Campanella, De siderali fato vitando, the astrological treatise recording the 1628 rite

stops.name: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, absolution and the school
stops.date_confidence: full liberty attested to 1629 (en.wikipedia), the school and the papal favour of 1630-1634 to it.wikipedia, Ernst (2010) and Headley (1997); Kircher's Rome dates are attested in kircher.journey.json but no meeting between the two men is documented, the overlap is [R]; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Absolved at last, he lodges in the Dominican order's principal Roman house, the convent attached to the church where he knelt to abjure thirty-four years earlier. He opens a school to teach his own philosophy, publishes revised editions, corresponds across Europe, and holds his place by the personal favor of one pope while conservative churchmen keep reading his older books. In November 1633 Athanasius Kircher is blown by storm to this city and takes the Collegio Romano chair; their Roman years overlap by months.
stops.quote: no one attains to the dignity of Hoh except him who knows the histories
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 233
suggested_refs: The convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome, his residence after absolution

stops.name: Marseille, the landfall in France
stops.date_confidence: flight attested to October 1634 (SEP; it.wikipedia); the common statement that he fled from Naples under Richelieu's protection is wrong on both counts, the flight was from Rome and Richelieu's protection came on arrival; day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: A new Calabrian conspiracy implicating a former disciple puts his name back in the files, and papal favor is judged too thin to hold against it. Cardinal Barberini and Francois de Noailles, the French ambassador, get him out of Rome, and at sixty-six he sets foot on French soil for the first time. He has been out of Neapolitan custody eight years. Accounts that have him fleeing Naples in 1634 are describing a city he had not lived in since the day the gate of Castel Nuovo opened.
suggested_refs: Francois de Noailles, French ambassador to Rome, who arranged the escape

stops.name: Aix-en-Provence, the stage on the road
stops.date_confidence: the overland route is documented (Bonansea 1969); the Aix reception itself is not independently sourced and is reconstruction [R]; the day is inferred from the route and is not recorded
stops.campa: He travels overland toward Paris and stops at Aix, where local scholars and members of the parlement receive the author of La citta del sole and the defender of Galileo with open curiosity. The stop is a stage on a road, not a destination, and nothing of what is said there is recorded. In Italy he had notoriety and nothing else. Here he has celebrity, an audience that reads his books without a tribunal reading them first and telling the readers what they mean.
suggested_refs: The parlement of Provence at Aix and its scholarly circles

stops.name: Paris, the reception at the court of Louis XIII
stops.date_confidence: attested (it.wikipedia; en.wikipedia); day unknown, defaulted; coordinates are the canonical atlas Paris pin, inherited byte-identically from adam_smith.journey.json and adnan_khashoggi.journey.json rather than the finer rue Saint-Honore coordinates
stops.campa: He is received with honor by the court of Louis XIII, and Cardinal Richelieu grants him protection and a royal pension. France is at war with Spain in all but name and finds obvious use in a friar the Spanish crown's Neapolitan tribunal held twenty-seven years. The welcome is statecraft as much as scholarship, and he takes it on those terms without complaint. He is given rooms, a stipend, and a freedom to publish that no year of papal favor in Rome ever gave him.
suggested_refs: The pension granted by Cardinal Richelieu to Campanella on the French crown's account

stops.name: Paris, the convent on the rue Saint-Honore
stops.date_confidence: residence and the 1637 Paris edition attested (Ernst 2010; Firpo, Bibliografia); month unknown, defaulted; coordinates are the canonical atlas Paris pin rather than the convent's own
stops.campa: He settles at the Dominican convent on the rue Saint-Honore and publishes there a collected edition of his philosophical works, the first time the system appears whole, in print, above ground, and under his own name. He goes on defending Galileo in print after the condemnation of 1633, a position that costs him nothing in Paris and would have cost him everything in Rome. He is sixty-nine and writing at a rate that men who have never seen the inside of a cell do not manage.
stops.quote: They think it also necessary that he should understand all the mechanical arts, the physical sciences, astrology and mathematics.
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 233
suggested_refs: The 1637 Paris collected edition of Campanella's philosophical works

stops.name: Paris, the horoscope for the Dauphin
stops.date_confidence: attested from court memoirs cited in Headley (1997) and Bonansea (1969); the future Louis XIV was born 5 September 1638, which the sources give as the occasion; coordinates are the canonical atlas Paris pin
stops.campa: At the birth of the child who will be Louis XIV he casts a horoscope and performs the ritual observances meant to secure the infant a fortunate destiny, the same art he practiced for Urban VIII in a sealed Vatican room ten years before and for the Calabrian conspirators forty years before that. He writes a poem for the birth. He once read 1600 as the year the old order would fall. At seventy he reads the cradle of the Sun King instead, and the crown paying for the reading is the one that took him in.
stops.quote: No one can exercise the function of a poet who invents that which is not true
stops.quote_source: Campanella, City of the Sun, trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 263
suggested_refs: Campanella's ecloga for the birth of the Dauphin, the future Louis XIV

stops.name: Paris, the death at the Jacobins
stops.date_confidence: date attested (it.wikipedia; en.wikipedia; SEP); the fate of the tomb is a stated gap, no source consulted in English, Italian, or French names a surviving grave marker or traces the convent's history past his death; coordinates are the canonical atlas Paris pin
stops.campa: He dies at the convent on the rue Saint-Honore at seventy, a free man on a royal pension, and is buried in the convent church. The building is pulled down long afterward and the remains are not recovered; no marked grave survives, and no source consulted follows the convent's history past this year. He was born in a shoemaker's house in Calabria and dies on the pension of a French king. Twenty-seven of the seventy years went to fortresses, and the city he described inside one of them has not been built anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Saint-Honore, Paris, demolished after his burial there

stops.name: Frankfurt, Civitas Solis printed
stops.date_confidence: first printing of the Latin Civitas Solis at Frankfurt in 1623 attested (en.wikipedia, 'The City of the Sun'); the Latin reworking is dated 1613-1614; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Twenty-one years after it was written in a Naples cell, and while its author is still in one, the Latin Civitas Solis is printed at Frankfurt, past the reach of any tribunal that could suppress it. The book travels where the man cannot. Readers who will never see Calabria or the inside of Castel Nuovo take up the city of philosopher-priests, common goods, and astrological marriage. By the time its author dies in Paris the book has been in print sixteen years.
stops.quote: a priest whom they call by the name Hoh, though we should call him Metaphysic. He is head over all, in temporal and spiritual matters
stops.quote_source: Tommaso Campanella, La Citta del Sole (The City of the Sun), trans. Thomas W. Halliday, in Ideal Commonwealths, ed. Henry Morley (London: George Routledge, 1885/1890), p. 225
suggested_refs: Civitas Solis, first printed at Frankfurt, 1623

stops.name: Naples, the philosophy that comes after
stops.date_confidence: Vico's Naples facts are attested in vico.journey.json, and the 1680s Investiganti trial likewise; the link back to Campanella's prosecutions is a pattern parallel and is reconstruction [R]
stops.campa: Twenty-nine years after Campanella dies in Paris, Giambattista Vico is born in the old center of Naples, in the streets between the Tribunali and the booksellers, and spends his life there working out a new science of nations. In the 1680s a Neapolitan tribunal tries the Investiganti circle of freethinking physicians for atheistic and Epicurean opinion, the same charge that took Giordano Bruno to the fire and Campanella to the veglia. The city goes on prosecuting its philosophers and goes on producing them.
suggested_refs: The Investiganti trial of the 1680s in Naples

stops.name: Stilo, the bronze in Piazza Carnovale
stops.date_confidence: monument attested to 1923, by the sculptor Ernesto Gazzeri (it.wikipedia, 'Stilo (Italia)'); month unknown, defaulted; the 1968 ministerial decree naming Stignano as the birthplace stands unresolved against the scholarly consensus for Stilo
stops.campa: Three hundred and fifty-five years after the birth, the town that produced him, expelled him, and was garrisoned against him raises a bronze by Ernesto Gazzeri in Piazza Carnovale. Stilo also keeps the church of San Biagio al Borgo where he was baptized. Five miles off lies Stignano, which a 1968 ministerial decree names as the true birthplace against the scholarship, and which sheltered him for three weeks in 1599 while Spanish troops searched the hills. Both towns claim him, and the decree and the scholarship have not been reconciled.
suggested_refs: Ernesto Gazzeri's bronze monument to Campanella, Piazza Carnovale, Stilo, 1923

stops.name: Trento, the oldest surviving copy
stops.date_confidence: the 1943 find and the 1980 restoration are attested (en.wikipedia, 'The City of the Sun'); Firpo's I processi di Tommaso Campanella (1998) is listed in it.wikipedia's bibliography and not independently verified [R]; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In the middle of a war, the historian Luigi Firpo finds at the Biblioteca Civica of Trento a manuscript copy of La citta del sole dated 1602, the oldest surviving copy of the text. It is restored in 1980. Firpo spends his career reconstructing the trials from their own records, and his documentary work becomes the thing that corrects the received account: which fortress, which torture, how many hours, who informed. The biographers have been repeating each other for a century.
suggested_refs: The 1602 manuscript of La citta del sole, Biblioteca Civica, Trento
Luigi Firpo, I processi di Tommaso Campanella (1998)
